metadata.file_name: 93. Liang et al. (2023). Using Process Data to Improve Classification Accuracy of Cognitive Diagnosis Model.pdf
metadata.title: Using Process Data to Improve Classification Accuracy of Cognitive Diagnosis Model

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The empirical analysis uses PISA 2018 computer-based reading data (12 items) from 79 countries, with response accuracy, response times, and mouse click/drag traces modeled jointly in a Bayesian hierarchical cognitive diagnosis framework. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or replicate weights, nor does it name any weight variables from the OECD PISA database; therefore, the weighting strategy is not documented. Because the model is fully Bayesian and estimated via MCMC in JAGS, the paper does not describe how complex survey design features (stratification/clustering) were incorporated into estimation. Analysts using the OECD PISA 2018 database should apply the standard PISA complex survey weights (and replicate weights if available) when producing population-representative estimates, but this paper’s documentation does not confirm that those weights were used.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study models dichotomous item responses using a cognitive diagnosis model (DINA/DINA-family) and models response times and action counts with separate measurement models; it does not use PISA plausible values (PV-based achievement scores). As a result, PV handling is not applicable to the dependent variables analyzed. The manuscript also does not describe any explicit missing-data strategy for the response/RT/action variables (e.g., exclusion rules or imputation), which is a reporting gap given that log-based process variables can be missing for incomplete interactions.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 computer-based reading assessment data for an empirical example: 12 reading items and 5 attributes defined by the 2018 PISA reading framework. The analytic dataset comprises 2,003 students across 79 countries (districts) and includes response accuracy, response times, and number of actions (mouse click/drag traces) for those items. The paper does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion rules beyond using the released PISA 2018 computer-based reading dataset and the 12-item subset.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Average attribute reliabilities: MHO-RDINA = 0.437, JRT-DINA = 0.454, JCDM-RRT = 0.494. PPMC: JCDM-RRT PPMC_RA = 0.551; PPMC_RT = 0.551 (MHO-RDINA: 0.584/0.567; JRT-DINA: 0.569/0.567).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Computer-based Reading the study leveraged item response accuracy together with response time (RT) and number of actions (mouse click/drag trace) to estimate a joint cognitive diagnosis model (JCDM-RRT) for attribute classification, finding that attribute classification reliability was higher for JCDM-RRT (0.494) than for models using no process data (MHO-RDINA: 0.437) or only RTs (JRT-DINA: 0.454). This indicates that incorporating readily available interaction traces and speed information can improve diagnostic measurement reliability beyond accuracy-only CDMs, though the paper does not document survey-weight handling or missing-data rules.

main_findings.target_variable: Person classification accuracy (pattern correct classification rate, PCCR)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Empirical-data-based simulation: PCCR JCDM-RRT = 0.5193 vs JRT-DINA = 0.4977 vs MHO-RDINA = 0.4860. Attribute correct classification rate (ACCR) mean: JCDM-RRT = 0.8335 vs JRT-DINA = 0.8230 vs MHO-RDINA = 0.8179.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Computer-based Reading the study leveraged item response accuracy plus RT and mouse-action traces within a Bayesian joint CDM to classify examinees’ attribute profiles, finding higher pattern-level and attribute-level correct classification for JCDM-RRT (PCCR 0.5193; ACCR mean 0.8335) than for accuracy-only (MHO-RDINA) and RT-only (JRT-DINA) baselines. This indicates that process data integration can improve individual diagnostic classification accuracy in computer-based reading assessments, though the reported gains are based on simulation using empirical parameter estimates and the manuscript does not report complex-survey weighting or missing-data handling.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Posterior predictive model checking: JCDM-RRT closer to 0.5 than other models (PPMC_RA 0.551; PPMC_RT 0.551). Simulation (empirical-data-based): item-parameter recovery best for JCDM-RRT in terms of RMSE and BIAS (Table 8 shows lower RMSE/BIAS across b, d, c, k, f, re, w compared with baselines).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Computer-based Reading the study leveraged RT and mouse-action traces alongside item responses to improve a joint cognitive diagnosis model’s parameter estimation, finding better posterior predictive fit and superior item-parameter recovery (lower RMSE/BIAS) for JCDM-RRT than for MHO-RDINA and JRT-DINA. This indicates that process data can strengthen both measurement model calibration and diagnostic inference, supporting the use of interaction logs for more accurate CDM item/person estimation, while also increasing estimation time (reported as ~6.5 hours for JCDM-RRT vs 1.91 and 3.58 hours for the baselines).

data.outcome_summary: The paper proposes a joint cognitive diagnosis model (JCDM-RRT) that combines three sources of information from PISA 2018 computer-based reading: dichotomous item responses, response times (RTs), and mouse click/drag traces operationalized as the number of actions. In the empirical example (12 items; 2,003 students across 79 countries/districts), posterior predictive model checking shows the proposed model has better fit (PPMC_RA and PPMC_RT both 0.551, closer to 0.5 than baselines). In simulation studies using parameters from the empirical analysis as truth, JCDM-RRT improves person classification accuracy, with PCCR rising to 0.5193 versus 0.4977 (RT-only) and 0.4860 (accuracy-only), and ACCR mean to 0.8335. The study also reports improved item-parameter recovery (lower RMSE/BIAS) and higher attribute classification reliability (0.494). Limitations include lack of documented survey-weight use and missing-data handling, and the classification gains are partly validated through simulation rather than purely out-of-sample prediction.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction cannot populate ml_techniques because the paper’s core estimation is a fully Bayesian hierarchical cognitive diagnosis model estimated via MCMC in JAGS (not a machine-learning predictive algorithm such as Random Forest/XGBoost). The schema’s ML-technique list is therefore left empty, even though the study performs predictive classification of attribute profiles within the Bayesian CDM framework.
